· Buddhist Festival: Chethiagiri Vihar is indeed a Buddhist festival celebrating the teachings and relics associated with Buddhism.

· Location: It is held at Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh, which is known for its ancient stupas and rich Buddhist heritage.

· Relics: The festival involves the worship of the relics of Sariputta and Maha Moggallana, who were prominent disciples of Gautama Buddha.

• The Braj festival in Rajasthan is held every year for two days in the Shukla Paksha of the Phalgun month, a few days before Holi.

The Mela is a religio-cultural fair taking place every year in Madhavpur, a village on the Porbandar coast, also known as Madhavpur Ghed in Gujarat. The village has temples of Madhavraiji, or Lord Krishna, and his consort Rukmini, believed to have been built in the 15th century. It is also known for its sandy sea beach, the turquoise waters of the Arabian Sea, a sea turtle hatchery and the Osho Ashram

The fair begins on Ram Navami, Lord Rama's birth anniversary falling on the ninth day of the month of Chaitra in the Hindu calendar, and culminates on Tryodashi, the 13th day of the month.

questions.solution:
The Champakkulam boat race is an annual snake boat race held in the backwaters of Kerala, particularly in Champakkulam.

The Somnath fair is associated with the famous Somnath Temple located in Gujarat. It is a religious fair that attracts pilgrims and visitors to the temple dedicated to Lord Shiva.

The Surajkund International Crafts Mela is a famous fair held near Delhi, in Haryana. It showcases traditional crafts, art, and cultural heritage, attracting artisans and visitors from across the country.

The Baneshwar fair is held in the Dungarpur district of Rajasthan. It is a religious fair dedicated to Lord Shiva and involves various rituals, cultural performances, and a large cattle fair.

Hence, correct matching is a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.

✔ Hampi Utsava, also known as Vijaya Utsava, is an annual cultural festival celebrated in Hampi, Karnataka.

✔ It showcases dance, music, puppet shows, and processions, celebrating the heritage of the Vijayanagara Empire.

✔ Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its historical temples and ruins.

Dunnapothula Panduga is observed in the state of Telangana in India. This traditional festival is particularly celebrated in Telugu-speaking regions and involves the veneration of bullocks and cattle, highlighting their importance in rural life and agriculture.

· Doljatra (also called Dol Jatra or Dol Purnima) is a spring festival celebrated predominantly in Assam and other parts of Eastern India like West Bengal.

· The festival falls on the Purnima day of the Phalguna month, coinciding with the celebration of Holi in many regions.

· However, Dol Purnima has its own distinct religious and cultural importance, particularly centered around the worship of Lord Krishna and the playful traditions associated with him.

These festivals and fairs are iconic cultural celebrations of Rajasthan, each representing unique aspects of the state's rich heritage. The Gangaur Festival celebrates marital fidelity and is dedicated to Goddess Gauri. The Pushkar Fair is one of Asia's largest camel and livestock fairs. The Nagaur Fair is renowned for its cattle trading, while the Urs Fair commemorates Sufi saints, reflecting Rajasthan's diverse cultural tapestry.

• The Sardhana Christian Fair is held in Sardhana, Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh.

• It is associated with Begum Samru, a historical figure who built the Basilica of Our Lady of Graces in Sardhana.

• The fair attracts pilgrims and tourists from across India.

· The International Kite Festival (Uttarayan) is one of the most famous cultural festivals of Gujarat, celebrated every year on 14 January (Makar Sankranti).

· Key features:

o Massive kite-flying events in cities like Ahmedabad, Surat, and Vadodara.

o Participation by kite enthusiasts from 40+ countries.

o Traditional Gujarati sweets like Undhiyu and Chikki are enjoyed.

· The festival marks the transition of winter to summer and symbolizes spiritual awakening.

Why Not Other States?

· Manipur - Known for Sangai Festival.

· Goa - Celebrates Carnival and Shigmo.

· Chhattisgarh - Famous for Bastar Dussehra.
Sarhul is a spring festival where Saal trees bloom with new flowers, and it involves worshipping the village deity, the protector of the tribes.

questions.question: Which Indian festival is a festival of lights? कौन सा भारतीय त्यौहार रोशनी का त्यौहार है?
questions.solution:
Diwali, also known as Deepavali, is famously known as the "Festival of Lights" in India. It symbolizes the victory of light over darkness and good over evil. Key features include:

• Lighting diyas (earthen lamps) and candles.

• Decorating homes with rangoli and colorful lights.

• Celebrated with fireworks, sweets, and family gatherings.

• Associated with the return of Lord Rama to Ayodhya (as per Hindu mythology).

Further insights:

• Holi - Known as the "Festival of Colors", not lights.

• Onam - A harvest festival of Kerala, marked by feasts and boat races.

• Bihu - An Assamese festival celebrating agriculture, with dance and music.

Makar Sankranti is the first major Hindu festival we celebrate. Also known as Uttarayana Maghi or simply Sankranti, this harvest festival usually takes place in the month of January and is celebrated in several states though under different names. In Himachal Pradesh, the festival is called Magha Saaji.

• In Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat, the festival is known as Uttarayan or Kicheri.

• In Odisha, it is called Makara Chaula

• In Bihar, the festival is referred to as Til Sakraat or Dahi Chura.

• Keralites refer to the occasion as Makaravilakku.

• In Karnataka, it is known as Suggi.

• It is known as Pongal in Tamil Nadu.

• In Maharashtra and Goa, the festival is known as Haldi Kumkum or Maghi Sankrant.

· The Gaan-Ngai festival is a major post-harvest festival celebrated by the Zeliangrong tribe, an indigenous community primarily residing in Manipur, Nagaland, and Assam.

· The festival marks the end of the harvest season and involves rituals, feasting, dancing, and cultural performances to honor their deities and ancestors.

· It usually takes place in December or January and lasts for five to seven days.

Lai Haraoba means merry making of the Gods. It is a ritual ceremonial festival observed by the Meitei community since ancient times.

Poush Mela is a traditional fair celebrated in West Bengal, particularly associated with Shantiniketan.

Key Points:

· Held during the Bengali month of Poush (December-January)

· Closely linked to Visva-Bharati University founded by Rabindranath Tagore

· An important cultural event in West Bengal

· Celebrates local crafts, art, and traditions

· Features handicrafts, local artwork, and cultural performances

· Organized by Visva-Bharati University

· Reflects the rich cultural heritage of Bengal

· Attracts artists, craftsmen, and tourists from various regions

The Hindu community mainly celebrates the Doongri festival of Himachal Pradesh, which honors Hadimba Devi, the wife of Bhim from the Hindu epic Mahabharata. The festival takes place at the Hadimba Temple, a holy site for the Hindus in the Kullu Valley.

· Tamu Lochar is the New Year of the Gurung community and is celebrated every year on the 30th of December in Sikkim. It marks the change of animal sign (lho) for the Gurung community.

· Tamu Lochar, also known as Tamu Losar, is a major Nepali-Buddhist festival as well.

· Tamu Lochar is observed as a public holiday in Sikkim.

· It is the start of the Gurung New Year, which begins on 30 December according to the English calendar and the 15th day of Pusa in Vikram Sambat(according to Nepali Bikram Sambat Calendar).

Further information:

The following are the list of festivals celebrated in Sikkim:

Maghe Sankranti

Maghe Sankranti, also called as Makar Sankranti in other parts of the India, is the first day of the tenth month of the Bikram Sambat calendar which heralds the onset of warmer weather. It is a major secular festival of the Nepalese. It falls on the fourteenth of January every year.

Sonam Lochar

The first day of the twelfth month in the lunar calendar is celebrated as the New Year by the Tamang Community in the state. The Tamangs celebrate this auspicious day with great joy and fervor.

Losar

Losar, the Tibetan New Year as per the lunar calendar, is celebrated across the state with great enthusiasm and gaiety. It is celebrated on the first day of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar.

Holi

This Hindu festival of colors symbolizes the victory of good over evil. It also marks the advent of spring and people of Sikkim celebrate it joyously with a splash of color. It is celebrated on the full moon day as per the Vikram Samvat Hindu calendar in the month of Phalgun.

Ramnawami (Chaite Dasain)

This festival is dedicated to the memory of Lord Rama. It occurs on the ninth day of Chaitra month (the first month of the Hindu calendar). The festival commemorates the birth of Rama who is remembered for his prosperous and righteous reign.

Good Friday

Good Friday, also known as " Holy Friday" is Friday immediately preceding Easter Sunday. It is observed by Christians all over the world as the day on which Jesus was crucified.

Sakewa

Sakewa is a religious festival celebrated by the Kirat Khambu Rai community of Sikkim. It is also known as the Bhoomi puja or Chandi puja (worship of mother earth). The festival begins on the full moon day of the Hindu month of Baisakh, which usually falls in April/May.

Saga Dawa

Saga Dawa is the most important religious day for the Buddhists all over the world. The day marks the birth, attainment of enlightenment and parinirvana of Lord Buddha. It falls on the 15th day (full moon) of the fourth Tibetan lunar month.

Id Ul Fitr

Id Ul Fitr is an important religious festival of the Muslim community that marks the end of Ramadan, the Islamic month of fasting. It is the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal.

Bhanu Jayanti

Bhanu Jayanti marks the birth anniversary of Nepali poet Adikabi Bhanu Bhakta Acharya who was born in 1814 in Nepal. It falls on 13th July.

Drukpa Tshechi

Drukpa Tsechi is the day on which Lord Buddha gave his first teachings to his first five disciples at Sarnath. It falls on the fourth day of the 6th month of the Buddhist lunar calendar.

Guru Rinpoche's Thrungkar Tshechu

Guru Rinpoche's Thrungkar Tshechuis the birth anniversary of our patron saint Lord Padmasambhava. It falls on the tenth day of the fifth month of the Buddhist lunar calendar.

Tendong Lho Rum Faat

Tendong Lho Rum Faat is one of the oldest and most important festivals celebrated in Sikkim by the Lepcha community. According to the Lepchas, Mt. Tendong had saved the Lepcha people during a great deluge which flooded the entire Mayel Lyang (Sikkim). The Lepchas celebrate this occasion to pay respect to Mount Tendong. It falls on 8th August every year.

Janmasthami

Janmasthami is the Hindu festival that celebrates the birth anniversary of Lord Krishna. It occurs on the 8th day of the Krishnapaksha in the Hindu month of Shravan which usually falls in the month of July or August.

Indrajatra

Indrajatra is a festival celebrated by the Newar community to pay homage to Lord Indra and his mother for rains and good harvest.

Pang Lhabsol

Pang Lhabsol is a festival unique to Sikkim and is performed every year to pay tribute, honour and to propitiate the protective guarding deities of Sikkim, especially Mount Khangchendzonga, the guardian deity of Sikkim. It falls on the fifteenth day of the seventh month as per the lunar calendar.

Durga Puja (Dasain)

Durga Puja is a Hindu festival which marks the battle of goddess Durga with the powerful buffalo demon Mahishasura. Her victory is epitomized as victory of good over evil thus, the celebration. It occurs in the Hindu calendar month of Ashvin which usually falls in September or October months.

Diwali (Laxmi Puja)

Diwali or Deepawali , the festival of lights, is one of the most important and popular hindu festival. It symbolizes the victory of light over darkness, good over evil, knowledge over ignorance, right over wrong and hope over despair.

Lhabab Dhuechen

Lhabab dhuechen is observed to mark the descent of Lord Buddha from heaven back to earth. He had left earth at the age of 41 to give teachings s to benefit the gods and to repay the kindness of this mother by liberating her from samsara. It occurs on the 22nd day of the ninth month of the Tibetan lunar calendar.

Teyongsi Sirijunga Sawan Tongnam

Teyongsi Sirijunga Sawan Tongnam marks the birth anniversary of Limboo revivalist and scholar Teyongsi Sirijunga. It falls on 23rd of December.

Barahimizong

Barahimizong is observed and celebrated by the Mangar community to worship their forefathers.

Kagyed Dance

Kagyed Dance is the post harvest masked dance to ward off evil and bring good fortune in the coming year. It symbolizes the destruction of evil forces by burning effigies made of wood, flour and paper. It falls on the 28th and 29th day of the 10th month of Tibetan lunar calendar.

Losoong/Namsoong

Losoong/Namsoong is the Sikkimese New Year which marks the end of harvest season. The Lepchas celebrate the occasion as Namsoong while the Sikkimese Bhutias call it the Losoong. The celebrations start from the 29th of the tenth month of Tibetan lunar calendar and continues for a week.

Christmas

Christmas commemorates the birth of Lord Jesus Christ and it is celebrated as a religious and cultural festival by billions of people around the world on 25th December.

The Ambubachi Mela (fair) is an annual Hindu festival celebrated at the Kamakhya Temple in Guwahati, Assam. It is one of the most important religious congregations in Eastern India.

Further insights:

• The Ambubachi Mela is celebrated during the monsoon season, usually in the Assamese month of Ahaar (mid-June).

• It marks the annual menstruation cycle of the presiding goddess Kamakhya. The temple remains closed for three days during this period, and on the fourth day, it reopens with grand festivities.

• The festival attracts thousands of devotees, sadhus, and tantrics from all over India and abroad.

The Bihu festival is celebrated 3 times a year in Assam: Rongali or Bohag Bihu in April, Kongali or Kati Bihu in October, and Bhogali or Magh Bihu in January. Each Bihu festival marks distinct agricultural stages and cultural festivities, reflecting the rich cultural heritage of Assam.
